btos.label: Real estate and rental and leasing (NAICS 53)

name: Real Estate
blurb: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest AI and now federally regulated under FHFA and CFPB quality-control rules; plus valuation, leasing, and property-management platforms with methodology disclosed.

points.desc: Census BTOS reports real-estate sector AI use directly from firms.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.name: AVMs are now federally regulated AI

points.name: CREtech and MetaProp track the proptech market

points.name: BOMA covers commercial building operations

points.name: Smart buildings close the operations loop

summary: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest deployed AI, and it is now formally regulated: federal quality-control standards for AVMs took effect in 2025. Valuation, leasing automation, 3D capture, and property operations are where AI actually runs; the regulator record and the platforms' own model documentation are the sources.

analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 28.9% of firms in real estate and rental and leasing reported using AI in the most recent period, up from 28.0% in the prior period, making measured adoption both substantial and still climbing. The sector's AI story spans a wide range of functions, from the consumer-facing valuation models that Zillow publishes for more than 110 million homes using a neural network architecture drawing on county records, tax assessor data, and MLS feeds, to the institutional analytics that HouseCanary deploys across more than 136 million U.S. properties using machine learning, image recognition, and data curated from thousands of sources. Opendoor carries this logic further, using pricing models to make direct purchase offers to homeowners, which puts real balance-sheet exposure behind the model's output in a way that consumer estimate tools do not.

The commercial side of the market has its own distinct AI stack. JLL states it has invested more in AI technology than any other real estate company, applying it across brokerage, facilities, and portfolio analytics. Building Engines, a JLL company, offers an AI-powered platform called Prism that delivers recommendations and automation aimed at cutting costs and growing net operating income for commercial property teams. Prophia uses AI to extract key lease terms from commercial documents and combines that extraction with expert validation to produce structured lease data, addressing what is one of the clearest production uses of document AI in the sector. EliseAI operates as an agentic conversational platform that handles leasing inquiries, schedules tours, follows up with prospects, and manages maintenance requests around the clock, targeting the property management workflow specifically. Matterport contributes a different layer, digitizing physical buildings into 3D models that support virtual tours, portfolio management, and integration with construction platforms such as Procore and Autodesk.

The most consequential regulatory development in the sector is the interagency final rule on quality control standards for automated valuation models, adopted jointly by the CFPB, FHFA, OCC, Federal Reserve Board, FDIC, and NCUA. As described by both the CFPB and FHFA, the rule requires mortgage originators and secondary market issuers that use AVMs in credit decisions or securitization determinations to adopt policies, practices, procedures, and control systems ensuring a high level of confidence in AVM estimates, protection against data manipulation, avoidance of conflicts of interest, and random sample testing and reviews. This makes AVMs the first category of real estate AI subject to binding federal quality standards, and it directly ties AI governance obligations to the mortgage origination and securitization process.

On the capital and ecosystem side, CRETI, the Center for Real Estate Technology and Innovation, maintains a network of over 500 investors focused on real estate technology and runs a zero-equity accelerator for emerging proptech companies. NAR REACH, created by Second Century Ventures and described as the most active venture fund in the global real estate technology space, operates a technology scale-up program that gives the residential brokerage profession a structured channel for evaluating and adopting new tools. CREtech organizes what it describes as the world's premier real estate AI conference, drawing 3,000 leaders and facilitating more than 20,000 pre-scheduled meetings, which reflects the degree to which the commercial proptech community has organized around AI as a central theme rather than a peripheral one.

For a decision-maker considering deployment, the sector's evidence points toward a few practical conclusions. The use cases with the clearest production track record are automated valuation, lease abstraction, leasing communications automation, and building operations optimization, each of which has named vendors with documented methodologies. The regulatory environment is moving: any organization using AVMs in mortgage decisions now faces binding federal quality-control obligations, and the consumer-protection framework administered by the CFPB adds a fairness and accountability dimension to valuation AI specifically. The sources are largely silent on sector-wide ROI figures, though Building Engines describes its platform as helping teams cut costs and grow NOI, and Matterport cites cost reduction and productivity improvement from real-time data integration. The honest read from the available material is that AI adoption in real estate is real and broadening, the regulatory framework for its most consequential use is now in place, and the remaining question for most operators is less whether to deploy than which layer of the stack matches their current operational gap.
